preamble: Palatalization (secondary palatalization or 'softening') raises the body of the tongue toward the hard palate during the articulation of a consonant, typically before front vowels or a palatal glide. It is phonemic in East Slavic languages such as Russian, automatic before front vowels in Lithuanian, and arises morphologically in Romanian, where plural -i surfaces as palatalization of a final consonant. Japanese realizes /k/ as [kʲ] before /i/ (kiri [kʲiɾʲi] 'fog'). It recurs across several Indo-European branches (Slavic, Baltic, Romance) and beyond, and is among the most widespread secondary articulations cross-linguistically.

examples.note: The soft–hard distinction is allophonic for velars: /k/ is realized as [kʲ] before front vowels.
An underlying word-final /i/ palatalizes the preceding consonant and is itself deleted.
Only the palatalized consonant occurs before /i/, so [kʲ] is often analysed as an allophone of /k/ there.
